input: The separation of propane from propylene by binary distillation is a particularly demanding separation, because the two components have very similar volatilities (a relative volatility of 1.82). In this case, the relative volatility is taken as 1.82, and it is assumed to remain constant over the whole height of the column. The product specifications require the distillate to contain 98 mol% of the light component, while the bottoms stream is allowed to contain only 2 mol% of the light component. Applying the Fenske equation to these specifications gives a minimum stage count of 13 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. It is important to note that this minimum corresponds to operation at total reflux, and that it represents a lower bound rather than an achievable design value. The actual design is based on a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio, and the number of stages that is required at that reflux ratio cannot be obtained from the Fenske equation itself. Instead, it is determined by means of a separate simulation. The Fenske result of 13 stages therefore serves as a benchmark: the simulation result must lie above 13, and the difference between the two indicates how far the operating design stands from the theoretical minimum for this separation. The result is a preliminary sizing figure of the kind used at the earliest stage of a design study, before any rigorous calculation is attempted.
target: A binary distillation separates propane and propylene at a relative volatility of 1.82, taken as constant over the column. Specifications are 98 mol% light component in the distillate and 2 mol% light component in the bottoms. For these specifications the Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 13 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The minimum stage count is the stage count at total reflux, and it bounds every operating design from below. A column at finite reflux needs more stages, by an amount the Fenske equation does not determine. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. The stage count at the design reflux comes from a separate simulation at that reflux. The simulation result is read against the floor of 13 stages: a count below the floor would show an error in the simulation, and the margin above the floor is the stage cost of finite reflux. The specifications are symmetric in form: the distillate is nearly pure light component and the bottoms nearly pure heavy component, so the separation is a sharp split at both ends of the column, and the stage count prices both ends together rather than either end alone. Nothing in the result depends on the feed rate or on the column diameter; the count is a property of the separation specification and the volatility alone. The Fenske count also fixes the scale of the separation duty. A minimum of 13 stages at a relative volatility of 1.82 marks a separation in which each stage gives little enrichment, so the operating count from the simulation is expected to stand well above the minimum rather than close to it.
